title: Real-World Evidence of Porto-Mesenteric Vein Resections with Pancreatectomy (PRIME Study)
authors: Kapoor D, Bhandare MS, Sharma A, et al.
summary: 1. The PRIME Study is a retrospective multicenter analysis from 11 high-volume Indian centers (2015–2023) evaluating outcomes of porto-mesenteric vein resection (PVR) performed with pancreatectomy and creating predictive nomograms for 90-day postoperative mortality (POM) and major complications (MC).
2. In 389 included patients, MC (Clavien–Dindo ≥3a) occurred in 32.6%, 30-day mortality was 2.8%, and 90-day POM was 6.4%.
3. Independent predictors of 90-day POM were Charlson comorbidity index >4, preoperative biliary drainage, preoperative radiotherapy, segmental PVR, and additional organ resection.

4. For MCs, the key independent predictors were ASA grade 3/4, preoperative radiotherapy, and additional organ resection, and the study reports nomogram performance of AUC 0.757 for POM (cutoff >1.79) and AUC 0.669 for MC (cutoff >0.678).

5. Among 263 patients with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, median overall survival was 25.01 months and disease-free survival was 16.72 months, with worse outcomes linked to perineural invasion/segmental PVR/margin positivity and improved survival associated with completing planned multimodality treatment.

title: ASO Author Reflections: Predictive Clinical Nomograms for Postoperative Outcomes Following Porto-Mesenteric Vein Resection
authors: Shrikhande SV, Kapoor D, Chaudhari VA, Bhandare MS
summary: 1.	This “Author Reflections” piece explains how pancreatic surgery with porto-mesenteric vein resection (VR) evolved from early skepticism to wider acceptance as outcomes improved and systemic therapy advanced.
2.	The PRIME Study reported real-world, multicentre Indian data across 11 experienced centres over 8 years, totaling 389 VR-with-pancreatectomy cases.
3.	Reported outcomes were comparable to global literature, with 30-day postoperative mortality of 2.8%, 90-day mortality of 6.4%, and major complications of 32.6%.

4.	Key predictors of worse postoperative outcomes included higher comorbidity burden, preoperative biliary drainage, preoperative radiation, segmental VR, and additional organ resection (with segmental VR linked to higher failure-to-rescue).

5.	The authors argue that predictive nomograms integrating clinical and radiologic variables can improve patient selection and personalized risk stratification, and future progress will likely be driven by “biological resectability,” big data, and machine-learning–enabled precision surgery.

title: ASO Visual Abstract: Real-World Evidence of Porto-Mesenteric Vein Resections with Pancreatectomy (PRIME Study)
authors: Kapoor D, Bhandare MS, Sharma A, et al.
summary: 1.	This ASOVisual Abstract in Annals of Surgical Oncology presents the PRIME Study, focused on porto-mesenteric vein resections performed with pancreatectomy and the creation of predictive clinical nomograms for postoperative outcomes.
2.	It describes an analysis of 389 cases from the Porto-mesenteric Vein Resection-Indian MulticentrE (PRIME) Study.
3.	The visual abstract was published online on 05 August 2025 in Volume 32 (pages 7469–7470), with the issue date listed as October 2025.
4.	Deeksha Kapoor and Manish S. Bhandare are credited as joint first authors within a large multi-institutional author group representing multiple GI and HPB centres across India.
5.	Overall, it serves as a concise graphical companion highlighting real-world surgical evidence and a nomogram-based risk-prediction tool intended to support perioperative decision-making.

title: Prejudice or Parity? Exploring Gender Bias and Perceived Disparities in the Careers of Gastrointestinal and Hepatopancreatobiliary Surgeons in India
authors: Uppal M, Mishra DS, Suman S, Kapoor D
summary: 1.	This study examines perceived gender bias and career disparities among gastrointestinal (GI) and hepato-pancreato-biliary (HPB) surgeons in India, highlighting how workplace culture and institutional factors can affect training, advancement, and leadership representation.

2.	Using a nationwide, cross-sectional online questionnaire distributed via the IASG database and messaging/email forums (open for 8 weeks in Nov–Dec 2024), the authors assessed demographics, work environment, research, leadership, mentorship, and personal life; 1425 surgeons were contacted.

3.	Among 190 respondents (26.8% female), female surgeons were younger and earlier in career stage, and they reported higher perceived differential treatment—especially from senior faculty and patients—despite comparable salaries.

4.	Female surgeons also felt they had fewer advancement opportunities, were underrepresented in leadership/mentorship networks, reported greater work–life balance strain (including family planning and maternity leave concerns), and were less likely to hold editorial board or clinical leadership roles (even where publication counts were similar).

5.	The authors conclude that meaningful gender-equity progress in Indian GI/HPB surgery will require targeted interventions—particularly structured mentorship and institutional/policy reforms—to improve advancement pathways, leadership representation, and workforce inclusivity.

title: Post-bariatric surgery nutritional supplementation: An evaluation of compliance and nutrient adequacy in the Indian patients
authors: Singh A, Kapoor D, Vats R, Goel D
summary: 1.	This prospective, single-centre observational study (August 2022–July 2023) from a tertiary hospital in India evaluated post-operative nutritional supplementation compliance and adequacy in 32 Indian patients undergoing bariatric surgery (21 sleeve gastrectomy, 11 Roux-en-Y gastric bypass).

2.	Patients received ASMBS 2019 guideline-based supplementation—70 g daily protein, 50 mg iron, 1200 mg calcium, weekly 60,000 IU Vitamin D3 and monthly 1000 μg injectable Vitamin B12—with monitoring at baseline, 3 and 6 months.
3.	Compliance was highest for iron and calcium (96.9% each) but poorest for protein (28.1%) and Vitamin B12 (43.7%); mean BMI decreased from 47 to 36.1 kg/m² over 6 months.

4.	Only Vitamin B12 deficiency was significantly affected by compliance, with non-compliant patients showing persistent deficiency (50% vs. 0%, P = 0.001), while other nutrient levels improved irrespective of adherence.

5.	The authors conclude that the ASMBS protocol is adequate for Indian patients but emphasise Vitamin B12 compliance as a critical modifiable determinant, recommending tailored counselling, cost-effective strategies and multicentre studies to improve long-term adherence.

title: Surgical Management of Postcholecystectomy Strasberg Type E4 Bile Duct Injuries
authors: Kapoor D, Perwaiz A, Singh A, Yadav A, Chaudhary A
summary: 1.	This original research reports a retrospective observational experience (Oct 2003–Dec 2020) focused specifically on severe Strasberg type E4 postcholecystectomy bile duct injuries, where the right and left hepatic ducts are separated at the hilum and outcomes after standard repair are often poor.

2.	Among 119 surgically managed bile duct injury patients, 16 (13.4%) had E4 injuries, most presenting with an external biliary fistula, and many had associated cholangitis and/or vascular injury, with repair typically delayed until sepsis/inflammation settled and nutrition was optimized.

3.	In the earlier period (2003–2010), Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy (HJ) was the preferred index operation, but primary patency was lost in 9/10 patients (often followed by cholangitis/stricture) leading to frequent radiologic interventions, redo surgery, hepatectomy, and even liver transplantation in one case.

4.	From 2010 onward, the authors increasingly performed upfront right hepatectomy with left-duct HJ for E4 injuries, reporting sustained patency without endoscopic/radiologic intervention at a median follow-up around 40 months, and better short-term morbidity compared with hepatectomy performed later as a redo after failed HJ (less transfusion, fewer major complications, and shorter hospital stay).

5.	They conclude that HJ alone in E4 injuries frequently yields poor long-term results and that, in selected patients at specialized centres, an upfront right hepatectomy with left-duct anastomosis may provide a more durable solution.

title: Hand grip strength predicts major complications following pancreaticoduodenectomy: A prospective observational study
authors: P L, Kapoor D, Singh A, Perwaiz A, Chaudhary A
summary: 1.	This prospective observational study (June 2021–March 2023) assessed whether the Modified Frailty Index (mFI) and preoperative hand grip strength (HGS) can predict outcomes after pancreaticoduodenectomy (PD) in 180 consecutive patients.
2.	Major complications (Clavien–Dindo grade ≥3) occurred in 10.5% of patients, and 90-day mortality was 3.3%.
3.	Weak HGS was much more common in patients who developed major complications (14/19) than in those who did not (28/161), whereas high mFI did not reach statistical significance.

4.	On multivariate analysis, weak HGS independently predicted major complications (adjusted odds ratio 11.52) and was also linked with longer hospital stay, higher 90-day readmission, and more overall complications.
5.	The authors conclude that a simple preoperative HGS test is a practical bedside tool to identify functional sarcopenia and improve risk stratification and counseling before PD.

title: Validation and Optimisation of the ISGPS Risk Classification for Postoperative Pancreatic Fistula after Pancreatoduodenectomy
authors: Kapoor D, Desiraju Y, Chaudhari VA, Bagwan AI, Chopde A, Namachivayam A, Bhandare MS, Shrikhande SV
summary: 1.	This retrospective analysis of 1422 consecutive pancreatoduodenectomies (2014–2023) externally validated the ISGPS two-factor, four-tier “high-risk pancreas” classification for predicting clinically relevant postoperative pancreatic fistula (CRPF), and specifically tested its performance in periampullary tumours (P-amps).
2.	The overall CRPF rate was 22.2%, with a higher CRPF rate in P-amps (25.8%), reflecting the softer-gland biology typical of periampullary disease.
3.	The original ISGPS model showed only moderate discrimination overall (AUC ~0.63) and performed worse in P-amps (AUC ~0.61), with calibration issues at higher predicted risks.

4.	In multivariable analysis for P-amps, soft pancreas, pancreatic duct diameter ≤3 mm, and BMI ≥23 kg/m² were independent predictors of CRPF, and these variables were used to optimize the scoring system.

5.	The adjusted P-amp–specific ISGPS score improved predictive performance (AUC ~0.67 in both training and internal test sets), and the authors conclude that site-specific risk models may be more accurate, though larger multicentre validation is still needed.

title: Primary Aorto-duodenal Fistula: A Case Report and Review of Literature
authors: Gupta A, Kapoor D, Vats R, Bukhari SN, Goel D
summary: 1.	Primary aorto-duodenal fistula (PADF) is a rare aortoenteric fistula between the abdominal aorta and the duodenum, typically requiring urgent diagnosis (UGIE/CT angiography) and prompt surgical or endovascular repair.
2.	The report describes a 64-year-old man who presented with bleeding per rectum and hypovolemic shock, with a background history of multiple myeloma on thalidomide maintenance therapy.

3.	After initial ICU resuscitation, he developed a major rebleed on day 3 with shock and cardiac arrest; bedside UGIE showed blood in the stomach/small bowel and a large third-part duodenal ulcer with transmitted pulsation but no active bleeding.

4.	CT aortic angiography demonstrated a large partially thrombosed infrarenal aortic aneurysm with a likely fistulous communication to the third part of the duodenum, and the patient underwent total endovascular aneurysmal repair (TEVAR) due to high operative risk.

5.	Following TEVAR, bleeding was controlled and the patient recovered without further inotropic support, ultimately improving clinically and being discharged on post-procedure day 11, supporting endovascular repair as a viable option in high-risk PADF patients.

title: Effect of Multimodal Prehabilitation on Muscle Mass in Rectal Cancer Patients Receiving Neoadjuvant Treatment
authors: Yadav Y, Gupta A, Singh A, Kapoor D, et al.
summary: 1.	This prospective observational study (June 2021–March 2023) evaluated whether a multimodal prehabilitation program improves muscle mass and postoperative outcomes in locally advanced, resectable rectal cancer patients receiving long-course neoadjuvant therapy, compared with a historical cohort without prehabilitation.

2.	The intervention was a ≥6-week, home-based protocol combining self-supervised exercise, nutritional counselling, smoking/alcohol cessation support, and psychological counselling during neoadjuvant treatment.

3.	Muscle mass was assessed radiologically and, among 100 patients (44 intervention; 56 historical), the prehabilitation group showed a mean percentage increase in muscle mass while the historical cohort showed a mean decrease.

4.	Improved muscle mass was significantly associated with earlier stoma function, earlier tolerance of soft diet, and fewer surgical site infections, with overall complications also lower in the prehabilitation group (29.5% vs 46.4%).

5.	The authors conclude that multimodal prehabilitation can improve physiological status and may translate into better postoperative recovery, recommending it be started from the first outpatient visit and incorporated into management guidelines.

title: Factors Predicting Prognosis in Metastatic Grade 1 Gastro-entero-pancreatic Neuroendocrine Tumours
authors: Pandrowala SA, Kapoor D, Kunte A, et al.
summary: 1.	This retrospective analysis of a prospectively maintained NET clinic database (Jan 2018–Dec 2021) included 100 patients with metastatic, well-differentiated Grade 1 gastro-entero-pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours (Ki-67/MiB-1 <2%) to identify factors influencing progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS).

2.	The median age was 50 years, 67% were men, and most primaries were duodeno-pancreatic (45%) or small bowel (27%); 73% had liver metastases, with liver burden categorized as high (>50%) vs low (<50%) liver involvement.
3.	Management was individualized in a multidisciplinary clinic, ranging from observation to surgery, PRRT, octreotide LAR, and occasional chemotherapy, used alone or in multimodal combinations.
4.	With a median follow-up of ~32 months, median PFS was 54.5 months, and estimated 3-year PFS and OS were 72.3% and 93.4%, respectively.

5.	On multivariable analysis, high liver tumour burden was the only independent predictor of worse PFS (OR ~3.44), and patients with extra-hepatic disease had significantly worse OS than those with liver-limited metastasis (5-year OS 70.7% vs 100%), supporting closer follow-up and potentially more aggressive treatment for these higher-risk groups.

title: Adjuvant therapy may improve overall survival in high-risk periampullary adenocarcinoma patients (The MIPPAP Study)
authors: multicentre Indian Cohort
summary: 1.	This multi-institutional Indian cohort study (MIPPAP) evaluated whether adjuvant therapy improves outcomes after upfront resection for high-risk periampullary adenocarcinomas (T3/T4 and/or node-positive), an area with limited and conflicting prospective evidence.

2.	Data from 8 centers identified 736 eligible patients from a larger pancreatic resection database, and a 3:1 match-pair analysis was performed using T stage, nodal status, and tumor subtype (ampullary vs bile duct/duodenal).
3.	In the matched cohort (458 adjuvant vs 163 observation), most adjuvant treatment was gemcitabine-based, and median follow-up was ~42 months.

4.	Overall survival was significantly better with adjuvant therapy (median 68.7 vs 61.1 months; HR ~0.73, p≈0.03), while recurrence-free survival did not show a statistically significant difference between groups.

5.	The authors conclude that adjuvant therapy likely provides a meaningful survival benefit in high-risk periampullary cancers—especially in T3/T4, node-positive, and ampullary subtypes—supporting its use despite the scarcity of definitive trials.

title: Surgery for Sigmoid Diverticular Disease—How the East Differs from the West?
authors: Singh A, Gupta A, Kapoor D, Perwaiz A, Chaudhary A
summary: 1.	This study notes that diverticular disease—traditionally common in the West—appears to be increasing in India, and it aims to address the relative lack of Indian data on the surgical management of sigmoid diverticular disease.
2.	Using a tertiary-centre colorectal surgery database, the authors report a case-series analysis of patients operated for sigmoid diverticular disease between January 2016 and January 2023.
3.	Overall, 102 patients underwent surgery, with 81 (79.4%) elective procedures and 21 (20.6%) emergency operations.
4.	In the elective setting, the most common indication was complicated diverticulitis with colovesical/colovaginal fistula, whereas in emergencies, intestinal obstruction was the leading indication.
5.	The authors highlight an “East vs West” difference: in the Indian scenario, fistula-related surgery is a more common indication than recurrent acute diverticulitis.

title: Women in Gastrointestinal and Hepato-Pancreato-Biliary Surgery: ‘Evening the Odds’
authors: Govil Sanjay, Kapoor Deeksha, Uppal Manpreet, Patkar Shraddhar
summary: 1.	This conference report summarizes a focused meeting held on 6 August 2023 at AIIMS Delhi (under IASG and IHPBA) attended by 26 women GI and HPB surgeons, aimed at openly discussing gender-related challenges and corrective measures.

2.	Participants noted that overt gender bias during training was often subtle, but women frequently felt they had to work “twice as hard” to earn equal trust, and the group highlighted unclear and inconsistent maternity-leave rules during surgical training.

3.	Practical workplace barriers were emphasized, including inadequate women’s facilities (changing rooms/toilets) and lack of properly sized gloves, gowns, OT dresses, and instruments designed for smaller hands.

4.	The report also addresses underrepresentation of women in surgical society memberships, conference speaking roles, and leadership positions—especially in the private/corporate sector—along with the need for networking opportunities and structural inclusion in scientific committees.

5.	The authors recommend standardized training expectations, supportive policies (e.g., creches/day care, clearer pregnancy/maternity rules, consideration of paternity leave), and a formal mentorship program through IASG/IHPBA, concluding that meaningful progress will require both institutional steps and a broader mindset shift.

title: Practice Patterns and Survival in Patients with Resected Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinomas (PDAC) — MIPPAP Study
authors: MIPPAP Study Group
summary: 1.	The multicentre Indian Pancreatic & Periampullary Adenocarcinoma Project (MIPPAP) analyzed upfront resected pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) patients from 8 academic institutions in India (Jan 2015–Jun 2019) to describe presentation, practice patterns, and survival outcomes.
2.	Among 288 eligible patients, R0 resection was achieved in 81%, and 75% received adjuvant therapy—most commonly gemcitabine or gemcitabine-based regimens.

3.	With a median follow-up of 42 months, median disease-free survival was 39 months and median overall survival was 45 months; where recurrence details were available, most first recurrences were distant (83%).

4.	Stage II/III disease and perineural invasion were associated with inferior DFS, and combining stage with perineural invasion stratified patients into distinct prognostic groups (best in stage I without PNI; worst in stage II/III with PNI).

5.	The authors conclude that resectable PDAC outcomes in India are comparable to published data, adjuvant chemotherapy remains the backbone after resection, and adjuvant radiotherapy does not appear to add survival benefit after an R0 resection.

title: Prediction of postoperative outcomes after pancreatoduodenectomy – What matters more? Radiologically assessed pancreatic morphology or body composition
authors: Kapoor D, Perwaiz A, Singh A, Chaudhary A
summary: 1.	This retrospective study analyzed 457 patients who underwent pancreatoduodenectomy (2013–2021) to compare whether CT-assessed pancreatic gland morphology or body composition better predicts postoperative outcomes.

2.	The authors measured pancreatic morphology (including a composite SA/MPD = pancreatic cut-surface area ÷ main pancreatic duct diameter) and multiple body-composition indices (muscle and fat parameters) from preoperative CT scans.

3.	Major complications occurred in 13.1% and clinically relevant pancreatic fistula (CRPF) in 9.4%, and on multivariable analysis high SA/MPD independently predicted major complications along with respiratory comorbidity, preoperative cholangitis, and elevated creatinine.

4.	For CRPF, high SA/MPD remained a strong independent risk factor and low psoas muscle density (PMD) also contributed, while body-composition measures were otherwise less consistent predictors than pancreatic morphology.

5.	The study concludes that SA/MPD most consistently predicts adverse outcomes (including pancreatectomy-specific complications and 30-day mortality), while measures like VFA/TAMA mainly relate to prolonged hospital stay, supporting SA/MPD as a practical preoperative risk marker.

title: Factors predicting 30-day mortality after pancreaticoduodenectomy – The impact of elevated aspartate aminotransferase
authors: Kapoor D, Perwaiz A, Singh A, Kumar AN, Chaudhary A
summary: 1.	This single-centre retrospective study analyzed 562 pancreaticoduodenectomies (2013–2020) to identify predictors of 30-day postoperative mortality (POM), with special focus on preoperative aminotransferases (AST/ALT).

2.	Overall 30-day POM was 3.9%, and deaths were due to both pancreatectomy-specific events (notably post-pancreatectomy hemorrhage and clinically relevant pancreatic fistula) and systemic complications such as respiratory, cardiac, and renal failure.

3.	On multivariate analysis, preoperative AST >106 U/L independently predicted 30-day POM (OR ≈6.14), along with elevated creatinine, preoperative biliary stenting, clinically relevant pancreatic fistula, and grade B/C post-pancreatectomy hemorrhage.
4.	Risk rose stepwise with higher AST, and an AST/ALT (De Ritis) ratio >0.89 was associated with about 8× higher odds of 30-day mortality.

5.	The authors conclude that unexpectedly elevated AST (and a high AST/ALT ratio) should prompt closer preoperative evaluation and optimization—particularly of cardiac/renal status—because these routine lab markers can help flag patients at higher early-death risk after pancreaticoduodenectomy.

title: A Cross-Sectional Survey to Assess Awareness and Perception to Clinical Research: Unbox Research
journal: Journal of Clinical and Preventive Cardiology
authors: Sharma P, Aggarwal R, Mittal N, Kapoor D et al.
summary: 1.	This article reports a cross-sectional online survey (25-question questionnaire) designed to assess public awareness and perceptions of clinical research/clinical trials (CR/CT) and willingness to participate.

2.	A total of 852 participants (median age 21 years) completed the survey, with >85% reporting awareness of CR/CT and hospitals, social media, and print media being the most common information sources.

3.	Participants most often associated clinical trials with the possibility of new treatment for themselves/others (63.4%) and new drugs being more useful than traditional treatments (52.5%), while fear of being a “guinea pig” was uncommon (6%).

4.	Willingness to participate was reported by about half of respondents, and the most acceptable involvement types included questionnaire-based research, research alongside standard medical care, and single blood draw/single visit.

5.	The main barriers to participation were safety/confidentiality concerns and fear, and the authors conclude that addressing these concerns is key to improving CR/CT participation despite generally increasing awareness and willingness.

title: Can we predict the need of nutritional support following pancreatoduodenectomy?
authors: Kapoor D, Barreto SG, Perwaiz A, Singh A, Chaudhary A
summary: 1.	This retrospective study of 562 consecutive pancreatoduodenectomies (2013–2020) evaluated which preoperative/intraoperative factors predict the need for postoperative nutritional support and help guide selective placement of feeding access (tube jejunostomy).
2.	Overall, 105/562 (18.7%) patients required nutritional support, delivered mainly via parenteral nutrition (14.8%), with tube jejunostomy in 8.2% and nasojejunal tube in 4.9%.
3.	On multivariable analysis, older age, serum albumin <3.0 g/dL, and higher operative blood loss independently predicted the initiation of nutritional support.
4.	For prolonged nutritional support (>7 days), the strongest independent predictors were preoperative gastric outlet obstruction and serum albumin <3.0 g/dL.

5.	Although tube jejunostomy was placed in selected patients, it was actually used in only 39.1%, with the highest utility in those with mental health disorders (83.3%), leading the authors to recommend a selective rather than routine jejunostomy strategy (especially for GOO, hypoalbuminemia, and mental health disorders).

title: Gastrointestinal complications after Corona Virus Disease-19 – A series of ten cases
authors: Chaugale S, Singhal V, Kapoor D, Singh A
summary: 1.	This case series describes 10 consecutive post-COVID-19 patients managed at a tertiary centre in India (Mar 20–Jun 10, 2021) who developed severe gastrointestinal complications: 2 bowel gangrene and 8 bowel perforation.
2.	Most patients presented with abdominal pain and were diagnosed on CT abdomen, typically during the third week of COVID-19/recovery phase.

3.	All patients had received steroids, and the authors discuss plausible mechanisms including direct viral injury via ACE-2 expression in gut epithelium, thromboembolic/microvascular events, and medication-related effects (including tocilizumab in a few).
4.	Operative management for gangrene/perforation was associated with very high mortality in this series, with rapid postoperative deterioration in most operated patients.

5.	In contrast, selected stable perforation cases with localized/contained collections improved with non-operative treatment (percutaneous drainage, bowel rest, and antibiotics), leading the authors to recommend a low threshold for CT imaging in recovery-phase GI symptoms and considering non-operative strategies when feasible.

title: Short-term outcomes following Hand Assisted Laparoscopic Surgery for left-sided colon and rectal malignancies
authors: Singh A, Kapoor D, Dubey S, Perwaiz A, Chaudhary A
summary: 1.	This single-centre retrospective study evaluated short-term postoperative outcomes of hand-assisted laparoscopic surgery (HALS) for left-sided colorectal malignancies in 580 patients operated between March 2010 and March 2020.
2.	The cohort was mostly male with a mean age of 61 ± 14 years, including 210 descending/sigmoid resections and 370 rectal resections.
3.	Key operative outcomes were favorable, with a 1.6% conversion rate, mean operative time 120 ± 42 minutes, and mean hospital stay 7.4 ± 3 days.

4.	The most common postoperative complications were surgical site infection (13%) and ileus (6.6%), with major complications in 6 patients; diabetes, hypertension, obesity, non-negotiable tumours, and longer operative time were linked to higher complication risk and longer stay.

5.	Oncologic quality was high with negative circumferential margins in 98.9%, negative distal margins in 99.6%, and average lymph node yield 12.6 ± 7, supporting HALS as a practical approach that preserves minimally invasive benefits while limiting conversion and margin positivity.

title: Enhanced Recovery After Pancreatoduodenectomy – Does Age Have a Bearing?
authors: Kapoor D, Perwaiz A, Singh A, Kumar AN, Chaudhary A
summary: 1.	This retrospective cohort study evaluated whether age affects the feasibility and outcomes of an enhanced recovery protocol (ERP) after pancreatoduodenectomy, analyzing 548 patients managed with ERP between March 2013 and September 2020.

2.	Patients were grouped as <70 years versus >=70 years (20.6% elderly), and the older group had more diabetes, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease and was more often monitored in ICU postoperatively.

3.	Despite higher comorbidity, length of stay was similar (median 8 vs 9 days) and rates of major complications and 30-day mortality were not statistically different between younger and elderly patients.

4.	Compliance with key postoperative ERP elements (e.g., early NGT and catheter removal, stopping antibiotics, drain removal, and tolerating soft diet) was comparable, and age treated as a continuous variable did not predict non-compliance with any element.

5.	The authors conclude that chronological age alone is not a barrier to safely implementing ERP after pancreatoduodenectomy and that routine protocol modifications for older patients are not necessary.

title: Solid Pseudopapillary Neoplasm of Pancreas – A 10-Year Experience
authors: Kapoor D, Dubey S, Perwaiz A, Singh A, Chaudhary A
summary: 1.	This 10-year study (2010–2020) from Medanta Hospital, Gurugram, reviewed 34 patients operated for solid pseudopapillary neoplasm (SPN), a rare pancreatic tumour predominantly affecting young women.
2.	Most patients were female (85.3%), with a median age of 27 years; abdominal pain was the commonest presentation, while 29.4% were detected incidentally.
3.	All patients underwent complete surgical removal with no deaths and no serious complications.
4.	Three patients developed recurrence (8 months to 8 years later) and were successfully re-operated, though one later developed distant spread yet remained symptom-free.
5.	The authors conclude that surgery for SPN yields excellent long-term outcomes, but what drives recurrence remains poorly understood.

title: Elective Gastrointestinal Surgery in COVID times
authors: Kapoor D, Perwaiz A, Singh A, Chaudhary A
summary: 1.	This study from Medanta Hospital, Gurugram, India, reviewed 314 planned gastrointestinal surgeries performed during the COVID-19 pandemic (March–July 2020), nearly half of which were cancer operations.

2.	To keep patients and staff safe, the hospital used a three-step screening process—checking for symptoms, COVID testing before surgery and chest scans when needed—along with separate areas for COVID and non-COVID patients.
3.	Serious complications occurred in only 3.5% of patients, which was no different from the previous year, and three patients (1%) died within 30 days—again comparable to pre-pandemic rates.
4.	No patient caught COVID after surgery, and six patients who tested positive before surgery were safely operated upon after a short delay and a negative repeat test.
5.	The authors conclude that with proper screening, careful patient selection and separation of COVID and non-COVID areas, hospitals can safely continue planned surgeries even during a pandemic.

title: Deviations from a clinical pathway post-pancreatoduodenectomy predict 90-day unplanned re-admission
authors: Karunakaran M, Barreto SG, Singh MK, Kapoor D, Chaudhary A
summary: 1.	This retrospective analysis of a prospectively maintained database (May 2016 to March 2018) evaluated how often patients deviated from an enhanced-recovery clinical care pathway after pancreatoduodenectomy and whether those deviations predicted discharge by postoperative day (POD) 8 and 90-day unplanned readmission.
2.	Patients were categorized by the number of pathway components deviated (none, 1-4, or 5-8) across 162 pancreatoduodenectomies.

3.	Deviations were frequent (91%), and a higher deviation burden was associated with greater risk of clinically relevant pancreatic fistula and delayed gastric emptying, as well as delayed discharge, higher mortality, and higher 90-day readmission.

4.	The overall 90-day unplanned readmission rate was 23.7%, and independent deviation predictors included nasogastric tube reinsertion, failure to start a soft diet by POD 5, failure to remove the indwelling urinary catheter by POD 2, and failure to stop planned antibiotics by POD 2.

5.	The authors conclude that post-pancreatoduodenectomy pathways are feasible, but early deviations can act as objective warning signals, with poor nutrition (low albumin) and cardiac comorbidity increasing the likelihood of deviation and downstream adverse outcomes.

title: The ‘True’ Definition of Sarcopenia?
authors: Kapoor D, Chaudhary A
summary: 1.	This letter to the editor responds to Mercan et al.’s April 2020 study linking CT-defined sarcopenia to higher postoperative complications after elective surgery for gastrointestinal cancers.

2.	Kapoor and Chaudhary argue that defining sarcopenia as the lowest quartile within a cancer cohort is problematic because malignancy itself reduces muscle mass and quality, so the remaining quartiles may not represent a normal reference.

3.	They highlight that the Asian Working Group for Sarcopenia recommends defining low muscle mass relative to a young reference group (e.g., below 2 standard deviations or the lower quintile), implying that comparisons should use healthy benchmarks.

4.	The authors caution that inconsistent sarcopenia definitions and pooling different major abdominal operations with different complication profiles can weaken conclusions about “life-threatening” complications.

5.	They advocate for country-specific normal reference data and further research to identify settings where interventions such as prehabilitation, nutrition, and exercise therapy can realistically improve outcomes.

title: Defining Sarcopenia in the Indian Population – a step forward
authors: Kapoor D, Piplani T, Singh A, Perwaiz A, Chaudhary A
summary: 1.	This prospective study aimed to establish Indian, sex-specific CT-based cut-offs for sarcopenia because muscle indices vary by ethnicity and Indian reference values were lacking.

2.	Healthy prospective organ donors (18–65 years) at a tertiary centre underwent CT-based assessment of psoas muscle area and density at L3–L4, with area normalized for height and density normalized for weight.
3.	Of 457 donors, 26 non-Indian participants were excluded, leaving 431 Indian donors for sex-specific analysis.

4.	The authors calculated thresholds using 2 SD, 1.64 SD, 5th percentile, and 10th percentile, found 5th percentile and 1.64 SD to be most concordant, and therefore selected 5th percentile as the operational definition for future studies (men: psoas area 220.7 mm²/m², density 0.56 HU/kg; women: psoas area 149.5 mm²/m², density 0.53 HU/kg).

5.	They conclude that defining Indian cut-offs is clinically important because sarcopenia correlates with frailty and poorer outcomes in chronic disease and GI malignancy, and they encourage broader regional validation to develop robust Indian standards.

title: Exemplifying direct inpatient cost for laparoscopic management of left colonic malignancy
authors: Gupta S, Singh A, Chaudhary A, Karunakaran M, Kapoor D
summary: 1.	This study from Medanta Hospital, Gurugram, India, analysed the direct inpatient costs of treating colorectal (bowel) cancer using keyhole (laparoscopic) surgery in 391 patients treated between 2015 and 2018.
2.	The typical patient was around 59 years old and stayed in hospital for about 6 days.
3.	The surgery and operation theatre accounted for the largest share of costs, followed by surgical consumables, bed charges and anaesthesia.
4.	Investigations, drugs and professional fees each contributed smaller portions to the overall bill.

5.	The authors highlight this as the first cost analysis for keyhole bowel cancer surgery in India, finding costs to be modest, though long-term cost-benefit studies are still needed to fully justify the approach.
